title: What survives when an Azure failure domain disappears?
description: Select a deployment topology, data protection policy, and failure. The model separates serving capacity from data recovery so replicas are not mistaken for backups.

topologies.label: Single zone
topologies.detail: One regional deployment with all serving instances in one fault domain.

topologies.label: Zone redundant
topologies.detail: One active region spreads compute and supported data services across three zones.

topologies.label: Warm secondary region
topologies.detail: A zonal primary replicates data to a smaller secondary that is scaled during failover.

topologies.label: Active-active regions
topologies.detail: Two zonal regions serve traffic concurrently and require explicit data ownership or conflict handling.

dataPolicies.label: Regional backup only
dataPolicies.detail: Backups protect historical state in the workload region but do not provide a ready cross-region copy.

dataPolicies.label: Asynchronous geo copy
dataPolicies.detail: A second-region copy reduces regional data loss but can lag the primary.

dataPolicies.label: Geo copy plus isolated vault
dataPolicies.detail: A geo copy supports failover while an isolated, retained backup protects against corruption and deletion.

failures.label: Instance loss
failures.detail: One compute instance stops responding while its zone remains healthy.

failures.label: Availability zone loss
failures.detail: Power, cooling, or networking isolates one zone inside the active region.

failures.label: Regional outage
failures.detail: The complete active region and its regional data plane become unavailable.

failures.label: Accidental data deletion
failures.detail: A valid privileged operation deletes state and replication copies the deletion.
